fenced_code.comment:
The DOCUMENT-LEVEL fence, anchored at column 0 (carve-grammars#138). An indented opener at the top level is literal text - verified against the pinned engine, ` ```js` renders `

js …

` - so this rule refuses it and `#fenced_code_in_container` takes over inside a container. Group 1 is an EMPTY capture rather than a dropped one: `end` closes on the opener's own indentation via `^\1\2`, and keeping the group means this rule and its in-container twin differ by exactly that one anchor, with every capture index and the `end` pattern identical. Two rules that differ in one place cannot drift the way two rules that differ in five can.

fenced_code_in_container.name: markup.fenced_code.block.carve
fenced_code_in_container.comment: The in-container fence: leading whitespace is the container's own indent, so it is allowed here and only here. `#container_blocks` reaches this; the leading-whitespace capture stays load-bearing twice over, since `end` closes on the SAME indentation via \1 and a fence inside a list item is indented. Reached only after the container's `end` has established that the line sits at or beyond the item's content column, which is the block context a line-based grammar cannot derive on its own (carve-grammars#71, #137).

heading.name: markup.heading.carve

patterns.comment:
A HEADING'S TITLE IS AN INLINE RUN, so a `%%` between backticks is code content and a trailing `%%` is a comment - `# a `x %% b` c` renders `

a x %% b c

` and `# a %% hidden` renders `

a

` (carve-grammars#601, markup-carve/carve#2682). The title carried one flat `entity.name.section` capture, so no inline rule ran inside it and the stripped bytes were painted as title. `#escape` leads: a backslashed backtick is a literal and opens no span, so a rule that read it as one turned `a \`x\` z` into a code span. The sigil forms come next, as they do in `#inline`: a `$` or `!` prefix owns the backtick run after it, so `#code_inline` alone would take the run and leave the sigil painted as title text. The verbatim rules sit BEFORE `#trailing_comment`: the earliest match wins, so a backtick run opening first claims the `%%` inside it, and a `%%` that opens first claims the backticks after it - the reading the engines give both ways. The full inline set follows, behind `#line_bounded_openers`, since the engine renders every inline construct in a title or caption.

heading.comment: A heading opens at COLUMN 0 at document level. Leading whitespace used to be allowed here (carve-grammars#71) because a line-based grammar could not tell an opener at a list item's content column from an indented one at the top level - it over-coloured the rare invalid case rather than under-colour the common valid one. The container split (carve-grammars#137) removed that constraint: `#heading_in_container` is the permissive variant, reachable only through `#container_blocks`, so the document-level rule can be strict. Corpus 178-a-flush-left-line-needs-an-open-paragraph-to-fold-into-6 pins the case this fixes: ` # H` below a nested item's content column is paragraph text, and this grammar coloured it a heading (carve-grammars#138).

block_comment.comment: A %%% fence line is a delimiter plus an insignificant tail (spec PART 9 section 28): only the leading run of % is structural, so `%%% TODO` opens and `%%% end` closes. %%% carries no info string - a raw passthrough block is a CODE fence with an =FORMAT info string - so `%%% html` is a comment. The end backreference matches the opener width exactly, so %%%% nests %%%.

braced_comment.comment: THE PAYLOAD IS NOT CARVE AND MAY SPAN A LINE BREAK. This was a single-line `match`, so a comment written across a break was not recognized at all and the markup inside it coloured - `a {% *b*` over ` %} z` scoped a strong run inside a comment, which is markup-carve/carve#1239 on the surface it was first reported on. 144 of 469 generated documents leaked before this (carve-grammars#320). Prism and highlight.js were given the multi-line reading in carve-grammars#312; this is the same fix on the TextMate side. The region carries the scope and offers no patterns, so everything between the delimiters is comment. A BLANK LINE ENDS IT, which is the bound Prism already uses for this construct - its pattern spells the body as a newline that is not followed by a blank line. A TextMate begin cannot look ahead for its own closer, because the regex sees one line, so without a bound an unclosed opener would scope the rest of the document: the failure the seven recorded unterminated runs in tests/lib/unterminated-fences.js describe. One paragraph is where the engine stops reading this construct too. The closer also takes any attribute run glued after it, unscoped: a delimited comment joins no attribute run, so that run is text (carve#2932). `contentName` plus delimiter captures keep the comment scopes as they were while leaving that run outside them.

line_block.comment: A line block (`::: |`) holds lines of text with hard breaks, so its body offers only the inline rules (PART 9 line block, carve-grammars#853). It nests nothing, so the first colon line of the opener's exact length closes it.
line_block.name: meta.admonition.carve

admonition.comment: Leading whitespace is ALLOWED, deliberately (carve-grammars#71). The strict column-0 rule makes an indented opener literal text at the top level, but the same opener indented INSIDE a list item is valid and common - verified against carve-rs: at the top level every one of these renders as a paragraph, and at a list item's content column every one opens its real block. List items now provide the block context needed for that distinction: their begin/end rules keep container-only block patterns reachable at the item's content column and close them before a below-content-column line falls back to document text. Restructured from a flat `match` into `begin`/`end` (carve-grammars#125): a div/admonition's opener and closer are on their own lines, so a per-line `match` left the body wide open to the full top-level pattern set. The closer backreferences the opener's captured colon run (`\1`), so it closes on an EXACT length match, matching PART 9's colon-fence depth rule (a longer or shorter run does not close it, which is what lets equal-length fences nest and `::::` hold `:::`) - mirrors the `fenced_code` begin/end precedent in this same file. `patterns` is the top-level pattern list minus `#frontmatter` (document-start only) and minus the column-0 `#abbreviation`, whose in-container form reads the body (markup-carve/carve#4874, carve-grammars#852); everything else - headings (corpus 170), nested admonitions/divs via the `#admonition` self-include, lists, blockquotes, tables - keeps working inside a div exactly as before.
admonition.name: meta.admonition.carve

patterns.comment: The body ends at any bare colon line, where the container closes it or opens a nested one. A fence open inside it holds such a line as code. No backreference here, so its scanner is compiled once.

admonition_in_group.comment: The generic container, reached only from INSIDE a composite figure group. Identical to `#admonition` except that its body offers `#admonition_in_group` and never `#figure_group`, so a bare `::: figure` at any depth inside an open group scopes as the generic container the clause says it degrades to (PART 9 §4c, GROUPS DO NOT NEST; corpus 318-composite-figures-9). Scope names are deliberately unchanged - it IS an admonition, and a consumer selecting `meta.admonition.carve` must keep seeing it.

figure_group.comment: Composite figure (PART 9 §4c, markup-carve/carve#1215). The kind word `figure` is RESERVED among the `:::` types: a BARE opener - the fence, its separator, the word `figure`, and NOTHING else - is ONE figure of ordered panels, not an admonition, so it carries its own scope and this rule sits BEFORE `#admonition` everywhere the generic container is reachable. The `[ \t]*$` tail is the whole distinction: an opener carrying a quoted title or a `[label]` (`::: figure "T"`, `::: figure [g]`) does not match here at all and falls through to `#admonition`, which is the generic Tier-2 container the clause says it stays. GROUPS DO NOT NEST: a bare `::: figure` at ANY depth inside an open group is a generic container, so this rule's body reaches `#admonition_in_group` rather than `#admonition` - that variant is the same generic container with `#figure_group` removed from its own body, which is what carries the rule down a chain of `:::` containers. RESIDUAL, written down rather than left to be rediscovered: a bare opener reached through a LIST ITEM or a BLOCKQUOTE inside a group goes through `#container_blocks`, which still offers `#figure_group`, so it over-colours as a group there. That is the same block-context limit every line-based rule in this file has (carve-grammars#71); tree-sitter-carve is where a real container model lives. THE SEPARATOR IS A SPACE RUN, never a tab (grammar.ebnf PART 7, MARKER SEPARATORS; corpus 254): `:::<TAB>figure` is a paragraph, so this rule does not claim it and the line falls to `#admonition`, which over-colours it exactly as it does today - a pre-existing trade this rule neither widens nor fixes. Trailing whitespace after the kind word is insignificant and may be a tab. The closer backreferences the opener's colon run (`\1`), the exact-length rule `#admonition` already follows. THE CAPTION AFTER THE CLOSER needs no rule here: the group caption is an ordinary `^ ` line one line below the closing fence, which `#caption` already claims at the document level.

empty_quote_after_break.comment: A quote whose every line is a bare `>` is no caption host (CARVE-P9-080, corpus 554), so the caret line below it is a paragraph. A line rule cannot see the lines above, so this rule opens on a blank line or at the document start and lives until the next line that is neither blank nor a bare `>`; only a bare `>` run inside it reaches `#empty_quote`. Below a prose line the bare `>` may close a quote that line continues lazily, so that shape stays out of reach and keeps its caption scope.

empty_quote.comment: The bare `>` run itself, past any blank lines, up to and including a caret line, which it scopes as paragraph text instead of `#caption`. It ends at the first other line, and `#empty_quote_after_break` ends there with it.

blockquote.comment:
The DOCUMENT-LEVEL blockquote, anchored at column 0 (carve-grammars#138). An indented marker at the top level is literal text - verified against the pinned engine, ` > q` renders `

A quoted line's own heading, task, bullet or ordered marker scopes as it does outside a quote, nested prefixes included, and its inline run is scoped (carve-grammars#683); one match per line keeps every inline span on its line.

patterns.comment: A CAPTION'S CONTENT IS AN INLINE RUN, the same reading and the same repair as `#heading` (carve-grammars#601, markup-carve/carve#2682). This rule was one `match` whose capture 2 took the whole content, and a capture cannot nest patterns - so a real trailing `%%` stayed caption text although the engines strip it (`^ cap %% hidden` renders `<figcaption>cap</figcaption>`) and a code span went unscoped. It is a begin/end rule now, with `contentName` carrying what capture 2 used to. The full inline set follows, behind `#line_bounded_openers`, since the engine renders every inline construct in a title or caption.

caption_label.comment: Leading whitespace is ALLOWED, deliberately (carve-grammars#71). The strict column-0 rule makes an indented opener literal text at the top level, but the same opener indented INSIDE a list item is valid and common - verified against carve-rs: at the top level every one of these renders as a paragraph, and at a list item's content column every one opens its real block. A line-based grammar cannot tell those two apart; that needs block context, which only tree-sitter-carve has (its #38). So the choice is over-coloring the rare invalid case or under-coloring the common valid one, and every block rule here picks the same side - the asymmetry this used to have was an accident of anchoring, not a decision. A caption is a label. A label (C2-B-234, carve#6508): it holds the lines indented past its marker, ends at a blank line, a fence, a table row, a `***` break, a block comment, a region marker or a line not indented past the marker, and a comment-only line between does not end it.

abbreviation.comment:
The DOCUMENT-LEVEL abbreviation definition, anchored at column 0 (carve-grammars#138). An indented definition at the top level is literal text - verified against the pinned engine, ` *[HTML]: HyperText` renders `

*[HTML]: HyperText

` and defines nothing - so this rule refuses it and `#abbreviation_in_container` takes over inside a container. Every following line indented past column 0 continues the expansion; a fence, a table row, a `***` break, a comment-only line or a line at column 0 ends it (C2-B-084, carve#6507, carve#6524).

definition_list_on_marker_line.comment: A definition list opened on a list item's own marker line (`- :: t`), which carve-js nests in the item (carve-grammars#844). Its later lines are the document-level entry's.

patterns.comment: A term is a label (C2-B-234): it holds the lines below it indented past its `::`, compared by the column the sentinel captures record.

A term is a label. A label (C2-B-234, carve#6508): it holds the lines indented past its marker, ends at a blank line, a fence, a table row, a `***` break, a block comment, a region marker or a line not indented past the marker, and a comment-only line between does not end it.

link_ref_def.comment: At document level a link-reference definition is flush-left. Indented definitions are reached through container patterns, where the container's begin/end rule has already established that the line is at that block's content column. The line directly below that is indented past column 0 continues the definition when it holds exactly the rest of its tail: a title, an attribute block, or both, at most one of each and in that order (C2-B-083, carve#6507). Any other line, a comment-only line too, ends it. A title alone on the first tail line ends the rule, since a child rule cannot end its parent: an attribute line below it reads as an attribute line, with the same scopes but outside `meta.link.reference.def`.

patterns.comment: A CELL IS AN INLINE RUN, so a trailing comment's run ends at the cell, not at the line end (CARVE-P9-041; corpus 518-a-trailing-comment-takes-a-tab-a-run-start-and-its-whole-separator-6). Reaching the line end swallowed every later separator in the row (carve-grammars#576). Leads the row's patterns so #trailing_comment cannot claim the position first.

task_item.comment: A task item is a bullet whose content happens to start with a checkbox, and ITS CONTENT COLUMN IS TWO PAST THE INDENT WHATEVER THE SEPARATOR IS - the checkbox absorbs the rest. That is measured, not assumed: carve-php and carve-js agree that a body line two columns in belongs to the item for every separator width from one space to five, where the same widths under a plain bullet carry the column with them (`-   a` puts its body at column 4, `-   [x] a` keeps it at column 2). A definition two columns under `- [ ] a` is collected exactly as it is under `- a`, which is why the checkbox counts as CONTENT rather than as part of the marker, and why `while` asks for a fixed two columns here while `#list_item` reconstructs the separator width from the marker line. The rule is a container in its own right for the same reason: a one-line match would leave the following lines to the document level, where a definition must be flush-left, and `- [ ] a` would lose the indented definition that `- a` keeps.

marker_line_continuation.comment: A `+` that is the whole rest of a list item's or footnote's marker line is the continuation marker too (`- +`, `1. +`, `- [ ] +`, `[^a]: +`). `\G` is where the container's opener stopped: a list opener has consumed its separator, a footnote opener stops before it. A footnote's `+` is a marker only when a flush-left line follows, which a line grammar cannot see, so it is scoped regardless.

list_item.comment: A LIST ITEM IS A CONTAINER, NOT A LINE (carve-grammars#94). It opens on its marker line, stays open across blank lines, and closes on the first nonblank line indented BELOW its content column - which is the marker's actual width, `indent + marker + separator`, not a fixed two columns. That column test is what lets the block rules inside it (`#container_blocks`) fire on an indented line without also firing on a top-level indented line that the language reads as text: `- a` followed by `  [r]: /u` keeps the definition, while `- - a` followed by ` [r]: /u` sits below every open content column and is item text, which is what carve-php does with both. THE TEST IS EXACT FOR A BULLET at any indent and any separator width, because a bullet marker is always one column wide and the separator is captured as whitespace, so `\1[ \t]\3` reconstructs the column count from the marker line itself rather than assuming one. Its limits: a TAB counts as one column here rather than advancing to the next tab stop, and the continuation line must repeat the marker line's own indent characters - the pre-existing `\1` convention, unchanged. The ATTRIBUTE-GLUED FORM (`-{#x} item`) is the one bullet shape whose content column this cannot count, since the block's width is not whitespace; it uses the MINIMUM content column (indent plus two) instead, which keeps the container open across a range where an exact test would have closed it - deliberately the over-coloring side, the same side every block rule in this file already takes. A marker line may carry several markers (`- - A` opens nested list structure), so the opener still scopes a run of same-line bullet markers, not only the line-anchored first, and the column test uses the OUTERMOST marker's column so a line at the outer item's column stays in the list. A BULLET MAY ALSO BE GLUED TO AN ATTRIBUTE BLOCK, and then the required space comes after the block, not after the marker - so `-{#x} item` and `*{.c} item` went uncoloured on a line that IS a list item, while the ordered rule beside it already had the branch (#126). The guard is that rule's, unchanged: content is still required past the block (`-{#x}` alone is a paragraph), and the block is spelled out rather than skipped with `\{[^}]*\}`, because a quoted value may hold a `}` and may escape its own quote. It is a LOOKAHEAD - consuming the block here would make this rule own those characters, so the attribute rule could no longer scope them. THE PAYLOAD MUST BE VALID, not merely brace-delimited: an invalid one means the `{` is literal content and the line is prose. `-{+a+} text` (corpus 90-list-item-attributes-6) and `1.{2=v} text` are paragraphs, while `-{} item` and `-{not attrs} item` are list items. A guard that accepted any brace run coloured the first two as lists. Identifiers are STRICT (PART 9 S14) and admit no colon, which is what carve-js does - Prism and highlight.js still admit one in their own attribute rules, a separate pre-existing divergence. A zero-width while condition checks the content column before child rules run, so an unclosed container cannot retain scopes over a sibling item.

patterns.comment: A glued attribute block keeps the task checkbox after it (`-{.c} [x] done`).

numbered_item.comment: AN ORDERED ITEM IS A CONTAINER, NOT A LINE (carve-grammars#94), on the same content-column rule as `#list_item`: it closes on the first nonblank line indented below `indent + marker + separator`. An ordered marker is not one column wide though, and Oniguruma cannot count the width of a captured run - vscode-textmate splices a begin capture into the `while` pattern as literal TEXT, so a backreference reproduces the marker's characters, never its length. The width is therefore spelled out: one variant per marker width, each consuming exactly that many characters and asking its `while` for exactly that many columns. EXACT for marker widths 1 to 5 - `.`, `1.`, `10.`, `iii.`, `1000.` - which covers every ordered marker in the corpus; the width-5 variant also accepts anything WIDER (`10000.`, `civil.`) and under-counts those by the extra characters, keeping the container open a column or two too long rather than closing it too early. APPROXIMATE for the attribute-glued form (`1.{#x} item`), whose block width is not whitespace either: it uses the minimum content column, indent plus two. Both approximations err toward over-coloring, the same side every block rule in this file already takes. Every ordered marker the language accepts is still here, not only `1.`: decimal, single-letter and roman, with `.` or `)`, plus the BARE DOT (carve#472) - `.` alone continues the ordered sequence, and is the only marker allowed to drop its value. The bare form is also recognised glued to an attribute block (`.{#x}`), which is how corpus 174-bare-dot-ordered-markers-3 writes it. MARKER REQUIRES CONTENT, AND SO DOES THE ATTRIBUTE FORM: `1.{#x}` with nothing after the block is a paragraph, so the glued-block branch spells the block out in full rather than skipping it - a quoted run may contain `}` (`{title="a}b"} x` is a valid item) and may escape its own quote, so a `\{[^}]*\}` run stops in the wrong place. Anything less was tried and each attempt traded one broken shape for another (#85). A ROMAN RUN IS CASE-CONSISTENT: two classes, not one `[ivxlcdmIVXLCDM]`, which matched any mixture and coloured `Vim. text` and `Mix. text` as lists where carve-js renders paragraphs (#118). `mix.`, `civil.` and `did.` DO open lists, so the fix is the case split rather than rejecting multi-letter words. THE PAYLOAD MUST BE VALID, not merely brace-delimited: an invalid one means the `{` is literal content and the line is prose. `-{+a+} text` (corpus 90-list-item-attributes-6) and `1.{2=v} text` are paragraphs, while `-{} item` and `-{not attrs} item` are list items. A guard that accepted any brace run coloured the first two as lists. Identifiers are STRICT (PART 9 S14) and admit no colon, which is what carve-js does - Prism and highlight.js still admit one in their own attribute rules, a separate pre-existing divergence. A zero-width while condition checks the content column before child rules run, so an unclosed container cannot retain scopes over a sibling item.

code_inline_multi.comment: Two or more backticks: inline code that may itself contain single backticks; closed by a WHOLE run of the same length. The guards are what makes the closer a whole run: without them `x ``` z` inside a two-backtick span closed the span on the first two characters of the three-run, the leftover backtick opened another span, and a trailing comment after it was scoped as code (carve-grammars#601). A LONGER RUN IS CONTENT, which is the reading Prism was given in carve-grammars#312.
code_inline_multi.name: markup.raw.inline.carve

code_inline_unpartnered.comment: AN UNPARTNERED RUN IS TEXT (C2-I-017, carve-grammars#933): a run with no closing run of its length opens nothing, and a `!`, `$` or `$$` glued before it is text too. Tried after the closed-span rules; it consumes the whole run so a shorter or longer run behind it can still open its own span. TextMate cannot see a closer on a later line, so a span wrapped over two lines of a paragraph is not scoped.

code_inline.comment: A DELIMITER RUN IS ENTERED AT ITS OWN START and closed by a WHOLE run of the same width (carve-grammars#601, the reading Prism was given in carve-grammars#312). Without the guards a single backtick could be one character into a wider run, which is content.
code_inline.name: markup.raw.inline.carve

raw_inline.comment: A code span glued to `{=format}` is raw output for that format (grammar.ebnf `raw_inline`).

image_empty.comment: BALANCED LABEL BODY. The spec closes a link label or an image alt text at the MATCHING `]` (grammar.ebnf `link_text`), and the scan is escape-aware. A `[^\\]]*` body closed at the FIRST `]`, so a nested bracket run left the whole construct unscoped - `![t[z]](/i.png)` is an image - and an UNBALANCED opener matched from the outer `[`, where the engine reads `[t` in `[t[z](/u)` as prose (carve-grammars#226). critic_comment.comment: THE PAYLOAD IS LITERAL AND MAY SPAN A LINE BREAK. The spec says nothing inside an editorial comment is parsed as markup and no escape is resolved. This was a single-line `match` whose body also excluded `}`, so `{# a } b #}` was not scoped at all and a comment across a break coloured the markup inside it - 87 of 286 generated documents. Same shape and same fix as `braced_comment`. A BLANK LINE ENDS IT, which is the bound Prism already uses for this construct - its pattern spells the body as a newline that is not followed by a blank line. A TextMate begin cannot look ahead for its own closer, because the regex sees one line, so without a bound an unclosed opener would scope the rest of the document: the failure the seven recorded unterminated runs in tests/lib/unterminated-fences.js describe. One paragraph is where the engine stops reading this construct too. AN ATTRIBUTE BLOCK OPENS THE SAME TWO CHARACTERS: `{#id .c key=value}` is an id plus classes, and a begin of `\{#` alone claimed it and every line after it. The guard rejects the opener when a `}` NOT preceded by `#` closes on the same line, which is what separates an attribute block from a comment whose closer is `#}` - and leaves a multi-line comment, whose first line holds no `}` at all, opening as it should. A `{#` FOLLOWED BY A SPACE names no id, so it is never an attribute block and opens the comment whatever its first line holds (`{# *b*}` then ` #}` on the next line).

bold_italic.comment: BOTH NESTING ORDERS, because the engine renders them identically: `some /*both*/ text` and `some */both/* text` are each `both` (carve 0.1.5). Only the canonical order had a rule, so the mirrored one fell through to #strong and came back a bold run containing two literal slashes - a reading that says the document holds something it does not, and one no sweep could see because the row sampled the order this rule got right (carve-grammars#375). THE MIRRORED OPENER NEEDS A FLANKING GUARD AND THE CANONICAL ONE DOES NOT, and that asymmetry is the engine's: `x/*b*/y` IS bold-italic and `x*/b/*y` is `x*b*y`, because the mirrored opener leads with `*` and a `*` glued to a word opens nothing. Same at the other end: `x/*b*/y` closes into a word and `a */b/*y c` does not. CONTENT IS NON-SPACE AT BOTH ENDS in both orders. `a /* b */ c` is `* b *` and `a /*b */ c` is `*b *` - italic runs holding literal asterisks, not combined runs - and this rule read both as one combined run until the two guards arrived with the mirrored order. WHAT NEITHER ORDER COVERS: a body holding the OTHER order's delimiter. The engine reads `a /*b*c*/ d` and `a */b/c/* d` as combined runs and both branches decline them, which is the under-colouring side of the trade on the mirrored side - carve-grammars#382. THE CANONICAL BODY IS TEMPERED (carve-grammars#382). The canonical body admits any `*` that does not start the closer, which is what lets `a /*b*c*/ d` read as the combined run the engine renders. The MIRRORED body admits no `/`: a `/` between two word characters stops the inner italic from forming (PART 9 §9 R2), so `a */b/c/* d` is a bold run, and any other `/` is ambiguous with a canonical opener (carve-grammars#882). The opener's `(?!\*[\s*])` is what pays for it. Over all 21,844 documents `x */ body /* y` for every body of up to seven characters drawn from `* / space a`, judged by asking whether the engine renders the WHOLE body as one combined run: strict was 440 over-coloured and 603 missed; admitting any non-closing slash is 5,091 and 161; the word-flanked slash alone is 510 and 461; the word-flanked slash with the opener guard is 226 and 461. The temper alone RAISES over-colouring and every shape it adds is one the opener guard refuses - `a */**a/a/* d` and `a */* a/a/* d` are bold runs in the engine - while the guard itself costs nothing, since `missed` is unchanged with and without it. TWO MORE GUARDS THE MIRRORED BRANCH NEEDS AND THE CANONICAL ONE DOES NOT, both found by probing the shapes where one order's delimiters sit inside the other's. A `/` before the opener makes the pair ambiguous with a canonical opener - `a /*/a/* b` is `a */a* b`, an italic run - so the left guard refuses it as well as a word character and a `*`. And the closer may not follow a `*`: `a */b*/* c` is `a /b/* c` and `a */*a*/* b` is `a /*a/* b`, both bold runs, while `a */*b/* c` IS combined - so it is the character before the closer that decides, not the one after the opener.

braced_comment_in_strong.comment: Inside a `*` run, an opener with no closer on its line does not open while a closer-shaped `*` follows: the run ends there (carve-grammars#461). The closer takes a glued attribute run as text, as in #braced_comment.

strong.comment: A `*` between two word characters before the first closer refuses the opener: no span forms (PART 9 §9 R2, `*a*b*`). A BLANK LINE ENDS THE RUN, because an opener with no closer must not colour the rest of the file (carve-grammars#393). This is the ONLY bare inline rule spelled begin/end rather than as one `match`, and it has to be: a TextMate `match` cannot cross a line break at all - measured on a two-rule grammar - while the engine does read `a *b` over `c* d` as one bold run, which this rule gets right and its four `match` siblings get wrong. So the two properties trade off, and the trade is what the blank line bounds: without it `a *b c` scoped the next paragraph and the heading after it, and now it stops at the paragraph. WHAT IT DOES NOT FIX: a genuinely unclosed opener still colours to the end of its own paragraph, because `begin` cannot see whether a closer exists on a later line and TextMate offers no way to ask. Pinned in tests/bold-unclosed-test.js rather than left silent. MEASURE THIS RULE WITH THE RAW TOKENIZER: Shiki reports the fix as having no effect at all (carve-grammars#395), so a test written against it would call a correct grammar broken.

patterns.comment: The empty `{**}`, a comment opener the rule above refused and an opener-shaped star are text, so the run closes at its first closer. A same-kind braced span nests through `#forced_strong` below (carve#2904).
A strong closer inside a later braced form closes the strong span and leaves that opener text: `*a {/b*/} c` is strong `a {/b`.
A bare run whose own closer lies only past the bold closer is text. A nested `{*...*}` holds its own closer, so the scan skips it.

strong_glued_brace.comment: Inside a bold run an opener-shaped star is text, so only a star glued to a `}` can still open a nested run. A full `#strong` here rescanned the line for a `%%` from every star.

italic.comment: ONE `match` AND NOT `begin`/`end`, DELIBERATELY, and the trade was measured rather than assumed (carve-grammars#397). A TextMate `match` cannot cross a line break, so this rule does not see `a /b` over `c/ d` as one run the way the engine does, and it cannot hold a delimiter standing after a space either. `begin`/`end` buys both - and opens eagerly, because `begin` cannot see whether a closer exists on a later line, so an opener with no closer colours to the end of its paragraph the way `strong` still does. Converted and swept over the 1,545-document corpus, all four bare rules at once: documents holding a run this grammar MISSES fell from 13 to 9, and documents where it claims a run the document does NOT hold rose from 3 to 35. The whole corpus contains two runs that span a line break. A false run is the worse direction - carve-grammars#324 and #325 both turned on that - so the `match` spelling stays and the missed multi-line run is the price. Narrowing the openers first (`(?<![\\w:/])` for the URL, `(?!_)` for the dunder, `(?!>)` for the arrow) took the false count from 40 to 35 and no further. The closer probe groups each non-slash run with its following slash and consumes the run possessively. The older alternative revisited the remaining line on every closed span; the grouping keeps repeated short spans linear while retaining the 256-delimiter bound. A plain letter or digit body takes a direct fast path with no nested inline scan, because that body contains no nested syntax; complex bodies retain the existing recursive rule.

highlight.comment: A BARE `=` THAT BEGINS OR ENDS A SMART-TYPOGRAPHY PATTERN IS NOT A HIGHLIGHT OPENER (grammar.ebnf, Inline parsing precedence: "a delimiter that begins a multi-char smart-typography pattern: `=>` is the arrow, never a highlight opener - the pattern is consumed first"). Corpus 386's third paragraph is the shape it costs: `Not an arrow: key => value stays literal, and p <= q is a comparison.` renders with NO mark, and the opener `=` of `=>` reaching the closer `=` of `<=` scoped the whole 68-character sentence as a highlight (carve-grammars#325). That is worse than leaving a run uncoloured, because the output then claims the document holds a construct it does not - the same reason carve-grammars#324 gave for the arrows. THE GUARD IS ONLY WHAT THIS GRAMMAR MEASURABLY NEEDS. The opener may not be FOLLOWED by `>`, which is `=>` and the tail of `==>`. It needs no guard against `<`, `>` or `!` behind it, and carried one for each until it was reverted and measured: vscode-textmate resolves by POSITION, so on `a <=b c= d` the typography rule's `<=` starts one column before the highlight rule's `=` and takes it. `!` was the last of the three to go, and it went in carve-grammars#374 rather than with the other two: while the typography alternation carried no `!=`, nothing reached `a !=b c= d` before this rule and removing the guard scoped `b c` as a highlight. The alternation carries `!=` now, so the comparison starts one column early like the other two and the guard stops changing any answer. What holds the shape is the pair that measures it - the `!=` row in tests/lib/constructs.js and `a !=b c= d` in tests/highlight-opener-test.js - rather than a lookbehind nobody can see working. Removing it also stopped an under-colouring a lookbehind cannot avoid: `a \!=b c= d` escapes the `!`, so the `=` after it is an ordinary opener and the engine marks `b c`; this grammar refused it while the guard was here. The Prism grammar still does, and still needs its own guard because Prism applies tokens IN ORDER rather than by position - carve-grammars#380. A leading `=` needs no guard either - the content class already refuses one. THE CLOSER IS DELIBERATELY NOT GUARDED AGAINST SMART TYPOGRAPHY, and the asymmetry is the engine's: once a highlight is OPEN the closer wins over the pattern, so `x =y z<= w` marks `y z<` and `x =y z=> w` marks `y z`. Measured against the pinned engine, both. AN ESCAPE IS A DIFFERENT QUESTION (carve-grammars#385): an escaped `=` is not a delimiter at all, so `x =\= y` renders `x == y` with no mark and this rule closed on it. THE BODY CONSUMES AN ESCAPE AS A PAIR (`\\.`) and refuses a bare backslash, which settles both directions at once - the escaped `=` is eaten before the closer can see it, and a body that could not hold one would stop there and never reach the real closer past it, so `a =b c\= d= e`, which the engine marks, would have gone from wrongly-coloured to uncoloured. The closer needs no guard of its own, and that is a consequence rather than a simplification: the body can only get past a backslash by taking the pair, so the position immediately before an escaped `=` is never a body end. #385 COUNTED THE BACKSLASH RUN IN A LOOKBEHIND INSTEAD, and carve-grammars#390 replaced it for two measured reasons. The IDE's TextMate engine refuses a variable-length lookbehind by not matching ANYTHING - no error, the rule simply goes inert and `x =b= y` loses its mark too (markup-carve/intellij-carve#117), which made this file unusable in a TextMate engine Carve ships a plugin for. And every bound is reachable: at `{0,32}` the guard stopped seeing the run at 66 backslashes and refused a highlight the engine marks. A pair has no bound. THREE SHAPES STAY WRONG, pinned in tests/highlight-escape-test.js - `x =<== y`, `x =!== y` and `x =a== y`, a closer followed by another `=`, which the engine marks and `(?![=\w])` refuses; widening that guard means letting the body hold its own delimiter. ONE SHAPE IT COSTS: an autolink or a cross-reference glued straight to a highlight (`<https://e.example>=hi=`) really does mark, because there the `>` closes the link rather than opening a comparison - a flat token map cannot tell the two apart within a fixed-width lookbehind, and this takes the under-colouring side of that trade on the ticket's own reasoning. ONE `match` AND NOT `begin`/`end`, deliberately: converting all four bare rules took corpus documents carrying a FALSE run from 3 to 35 to recover 4 missed ones. The measurement and the reasoning are on `italic` (carve-grammars#397).

include_directive.comment: Reserved processor syntax `{{ path #section @key:value }}` (PART 9 section 19, grammar.ebnf `include_directive`). The core leaves it literal and a processor expands it only when a host supplies a resolver, but a grammar that does not know the shape does not leave it alone: its own selector is spelled with other constructs, so `#section` was claimed by `#tag` and an option slot by `#mention`. Scoped BY PART rather than as one run - the enclosing match is what keeps the tag and mention rules out, so there is nothing to gain by painting the whole thing one colour, and a reader wants the path to look like a path. The padding is a RUN of spaces, one required on each side; a tab is path content, not padding (CARVE-P7-001), and a part that is neither a section nor an option is left unscoped rather than refused, matching the processor, which leaves a malformed directive as text. An option value is an `attribute_value`, so it may be QUOTED (either quote, backslash escapes inside) and then carries spaces; an unterminated quote falls back to the unquoted run and stops at the space (carve-grammars#409). A PART ADMITS A `}` INSIDE A QUOTED RUN, because `quoted_value` does (`character - '"' - '\' - newline`): a part run spelled `[^\s}]+` stopped at the brace and killed the WHOLE match, so `{{ ch.crv @label:"a}b" }}` carried no scope anywhere on the line (carve-grammars#412). THE QUOTE DECIDES THE BRANCH - a quote's two alternatives carry lookaheads that negate each other, so exactly one is ever viable and the engine has no second path to re-enter, and the ordinary class excludes both quote characters so nothing else can claim one. That is what keeps the scan linear; it is spelled the same way in the Prism grammar rather than as Oniguruma's `(?>...)`, so the two surfaces stay comparable. A quoted run MAY hold the `}}` pair, and the directive's closer is the first pair OUTSIDE one (markup-carve/carve#2013, superseding the `\}(?!\})` bound of carve-grammars#413). It is the QUOTE'S TERMINATION that decides where the directive ends, not the pair: `{{ ch.crv @label:"a }} more" }} end` closes at the SECOND pair because the run is terminated, while an unterminated quote opens no run, takes the negative branch, and leaves the closer at the first pair - which is what still leaves a malformed directive as text. AN OPTION NEEDS NO WHITESPACE BEFORE ITS `@`, in every position (spec `include_options`): the bare path stops at `@` and a section name holds none, so an option may butt onto either slot (`{{ c.crv@shift:1 }}`, `{{ c.crv #Alpha@shift:1 }}`). It is spelled as its own optional run gated on a `@` lookahead rather than by relaxing the separator to `[ \t]*`, which would let two adjacent runs split a part in more than one way and make the scan backtrack exponentially on a line with no closer. AN UNQUOTED OPTION VALUE ENDS AT THE NEXT MARKER: `include_unquoted_value` is `unquoted_value` less the `@`, so `@shift:1@lines:1-8` is two options and never one whose value is `1@lines:1-8`; a value that needs an `@` takes the quoted form.

tag.comment: A mention or tag name (C2-I-092): runs of letters, digits, `_` and `-` joined by single dots, holding a letter, not ending in a hyphen. A run directly followed by a Unicode letter, number or mark is text. The mention and heading_tag rules share the name.

heading_tag.comment: Used only inside `heading` (carve-grammars#125), not the shared `#tag` include: a heading's own inline set does not carry `#cross_ref`, so without this guard a heading cross-reference's `#id` (`</#id>`, grammar.ebnf `auto_text_link`) would be wrongly claimed as a tag - corpus 118 pins `# A </#a>` staying unscoped as a whole. `#cross_ref` is not added here instead because that would mean modeling the full cross-reference construct (and its `>` closer) inside headings, well past this ticket's scope; excluding the one shape that collides is the narrower fix.

line_bounded_openers.comment: Openers in a one-line block whose closer is not on the line, consumed as text: a `*`, and a `{` that would open an attribute block, a `{#` or `{%` comment. A heading or caption takes no attribute block of its own; a valid one that attaches to nothing is consumed before this as one literal atom (C2-I-035). A `{` glued to an inline host is that host's attribute block, which a title takes (`# *a b*{.q}`, carve-grammars#882).

opaque_destination.comment: A link destination or an autolink, consumed whole so a delimiter inside it cannot close the enclosing run (PART 9 section 9 E2a). Same atom as the bare `match` rules.

patterns.comment: A label that is none leaves the bracket text, and no span or link opens at it (C2-I-079, C2-I-087).

A hyphen run after whitespace, the line start or an opening ( " ' that itself follows one, and before any other character, is a command-line flag and stays text (CARVE-P3-021, carve-grammars#833). Consumed whole so no part of it reads as a dash.

math_inline_multi.comment: A widened run: the sigil owns the whole backtick run, which a longer run inside does not close (corpus 168).

literal_inline_multi.comment: A WHOLE RUN CLOSES IT, the guard #code_inline_multi carries and for the same reason (carve-grammars#601): without it a two-backtick literal closed on the first two characters of a three-backtick run, the leftover backtick opened an unpartnered span, and the trailing comment after it scoped as code. This rule leads `#blockquote` at every site that includes it, and the marker run is capture 1 so it keeps its quote scope - tree-sitter-carve splits it the same way, with the `fenced_comment_block` inside the quote's `content` beside the `block_quote_marker`. The end has TWO branches. The first is the closer, which repeats the opener's MARKER RUN as well as its fence width, so a fence opened at `> > ` is not closed at `> `. The second is a zero-width quote boundary: an UNMARKED line is where the quote can end, and the engine degrades an unclosed opener to a line comment rather than hiding anything (`> %%%` / `> c` / blank line leaves `c` VISIBLE). Unlike the Prism and highlight.js grammars this one cannot demand the closer up front - a TextMate begin sees one line - so an unclosed opener still hides the rest of its own quote here; the boundary branch is what keeps that from reaching the document below it. Anchored at COLUMN 0 for the same reason `#blockquote` is (carve-grammars#138): an indented marker at the top level is literal text, ` > %%%` renders `

> ...

` against the pinned engine, so `#block_comment_on_quote_marker_line_in_container` takes over inside a container.

Reached from `#container_blocks`, whose `end` has already established that an indented line inside the container sits at or beyond the item's content column.

It LEADS `#blockquote_on_marker_line` in `#container_blocks`, which would otherwise take the same position and leave the fence to `#trailing_comment` as a LINE comment, with the hidden body coming back as live syntax. patterns.comment:
A HEADING'S TITLE IS AN INLINE RUN, so a `%%` between backticks is code content and a trailing `%%` is a comment - `# a `x %% b` c` renders `

a x %% b c

` and `# a %% hidden` renders `

a

` (carve-grammars#601, markup-carve/carve#2682). The title carried one flat `entity.name.section` capture, so no inline rule ran inside it and the stripped bytes were painted as title. `#escape` leads: a backslashed backtick is a literal and opens no span, so a rule that read it as one turned `a \`x\` z` into a code span. The sigil forms come next, as they do in `#inline`: a `$` or `!` prefix owns the backtick run after it, so `#code_inline` alone would take the run and leave the sigil painted as title text. The verbatim rules sit BEFORE `#trailing_comment`: the earliest match wins, so a backtick run opening first claims the `%%` inside it, and a `%%` that opens first claims the backticks after it - the reading the engines give both ways. The full inline set follows, behind `#line_bounded_openers`, since the engine renders every inline construct in a title or caption.

heading_on_marker_line.comment: A heading may open on a list item's marker line (`- # Title`, `1. ## Sub`, `- [ ] # T`): carve-js next2 renders it as a heading inside the item (carve-grammars#945). `#heading_in_container` is anchored on ^ and cannot reach text after the marker, so this one is anchored on \G after the marker's separator. A heading is a label (C2-B-234): it holds the lines below it indented past its marker. A capture per marker column (1 to 24) lets the end compare the indent; the next line at the item's content column is a new block. `- #tag` has no space after the hashes and stays a tag.
